facts.text: On 14 November 2008 India's Moon Impact Probe left the Chandrayaan-1 orbiter and fell to the surface near Shackleton crater, the first Indian object to reach the Moon.
It carried a video camera, a radar altimeter and a mass spectrometer that sampled the thin lunar atmosphere during the descent of about 25 minutes.
The probe was not built to survive: it hit the surface and the impact point is only known from its tracking.
facts.source_name: List of artificial objects on the Moon

facts.text: On 9 October 2009 the spent Centaur rocket stage of NASA's LCROSS mission hit the permanently shadowed floor of Cabeus crater to throw up material for analysis.
The plume contained water: about 5.6 percent of the ejected soil was water ice (Colaprete et al., Science 2010).
The impactor weighed about 2,300 kg and struck at roughly 2.5 km/s, about 2.5 times faster than a rifle bullet.
About four minutes behind the Centaur, the LCROSS shepherding spacecraft flew through the debris plume, measured it, and sent the data to Earth before it hit too.
Its spectrometers found water vapor and ice grains, plus hydrogen gas, carbon monoxide and other volatiles.
Intuitive Machines' Athena landed near Mons Mouton in the south polar region on 6 March 2025, closer to the pole than any earlier lander.
It came to rest on its side in a crater and its battery ran out within a day, so the mission ended early. The position here is approximate.
Odysseus touched down near Malapert A on 22 February 2024: the first US landing since Apollo 17 in 1972 and the first by a private company.
It caught a footpad on the ground and tipped onto its side. NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed it two days later.
On 7 September 2019 India's Vikram lander lost contact about 2 km above the surface during its final descent and crashed.
facts.source_name: NASA: LRO spots Vikram crash site

facts.text: LRO found the debris field months later; the first lead came from an amateur, engineer Shanmuga Subramanian.
facts.source_name: NASA: LRO spots Vikram crash site

facts.text: On 23 August 2023 India made the first soft landing near the lunar south polar region, at 69.4 degrees south.
The Pragyan rover drove about 100 m from the lander and measured sulfur in the soil with its X-ray spectrometer.
Russia's Luna 25, its first lunar probe since 1976, crashed on 19 August 2023 after an orbit maneuver went wrong, aiming for the south polar region.
LRO later photographed a new crater about 10 m wide at the crash site.
facts.source_name: List of artificial objects on the Moon

sites.title: Apollo 11 - Tranquility Base
left: Plaque: We came in peace for all mankind

facts.text: Armstrong and Aldrin spent 21 h 36 min on the surface on 20-21 July 1969, with one moonwalk of about 2 h 31 min.
The laser reflector they placed is still used: observatories on Earth time laser echoes to measure the Moon's distance to the millimeter.
The ascent engine blast knocked the flag over; the descent stage still stands as the launch pad.

sites.title: Apollo 12 - Ocean of Storms
left: ALSEP science station with a nuclear power unit

facts.text: Conrad and Bean landed about 155 m from the Surveyor 3 probe, a precision landing that proved Apollo could target a spot.
They cut off Surveyor 3's camera and parts and brought them home to study how materials aged on the Moon.
Their ALSEP was the first to run on a radioisotope generator and sent data until 1977.
Shepard and Mitchell climbed toward Cone crater hauling a two-wheeled equipment cart nicknamed the lunar rickshaw.
At the end Shepard hit two golf balls with a makeshift 6-iron head.
They returned 42 kg of rock from the Fra Mauro formation, ejecta from the Imbrium impact.
Scott and Irwin drove the first Lunar Roving Vehicle about 28 km over three moonwalks beside the Hadley Rille canyon.
Their retroreflector has 300 prisms, three times larger than the Apollo 11 and 14 arrays, and is the most used by ranging stations.
They left a small aluminum figure, Fallen Astronaut, with a plaque naming astronauts and cosmonauts who died in the space race.
Young and Duke were the first to land in the lunar highlands, expecting volcanic rock; the samples turned out to be impact breccias.
They brought back 95 kg of samples and drove the rover about 27 km.
Duke left a photo of his family on the surface; it is still there, bleached by sunlight.

sites.title: Apollo 17 - Taurus-Littrow
left: Plaque: Here man completed his first explorations of the Moon

facts.text: Cernan and Schmitt, a geologist, were the last humans on the Moon, leaving on 14 December 1972.
They drove about 36 km, the farthest of any crew, and found orange volcanic glass soil at Shorty crater.
They returned 110 kg of samples, the most of any mission.
On 2 June 1966 it made the first US soft landing on the Moon, proving the ground could carry a spacecraft.
It sent back more than 11,000 pictures before the lunar night ended its mission.

sites.title: Surveyor 3
left: Surveyor lander (camera and parts were taken home by Apollo 12)

facts.text: Apollo 12's crew walked to it in November 1969 and cut off the TV camera and other parts for study on Earth.
It is the only spacecraft on the Moon that humans have visited.
Its alpha-scattering instrument made the first chemical analysis of lunar soil on the spot, showing it was basalt-like.
It landed in Mare Tranquillitatis, near where Apollo 11 would land two years later.

sites.title: Surveyor 6
left: Surveyor lander (moved 2.4 m from its first spot)

facts.text: On 17 November 1967 it fired its engines for 2.5 seconds, lifted about 4 m and landed 2.4 m away, the first liftoff from another world.
The hop let engineers photograph its own landing footprints and measure the soil.
The last Surveyor landed in the highlands beside Tycho crater in January 1968.
Two laser beams fired from Earth were seen by its camera, the first lasers detected on the Moon.
On 3 February 1966 it made the first soft landing on the Moon and sent the first pictures from the surface.
Its landing proved the surface was solid enough for a lander, not deep dust.
The first remote-controlled rover on another world drove 10.5 km over 11 months, steered by a crew on Earth.
LRO photographed it in 2010 and a laser echo from its reflector was received that April, after decades of being lost.
It drove about 39 km in four months in Le Monnier crater, a distance record for another world that stood for decades.
It stopped after the lid fell on dust-covered radiators and overheated it.

sites.title: Luna 16
left: Descent stage (the return capsule brought 101 g of soil to Earth)

facts.text: In September 1970 it drilled into Mare Fecunditatis and returned 101 g of soil, the first robotic sample return from another world.

sites.title: Luna 24
left: Descent stage (the return capsule brought 170 g of core to Earth)

facts.text: The last Soviet lunar mission drilled a 2 m core in Mare Crisium and returned 170 g of it in August 1976.
After it, no spacecraft softly landed on the Moon for 37 years until Chang'e 3.
On 14 December 2013 China made the first soft landing on the Moon in 37 years, in Mare Imbrium.
Yutu's ground-penetrating radar found distinct layers of lava flows beneath the surface.
On 3 January 2019 it made the first soft landing on the far side of the Moon, in Von Karman crater, with a relay satellite to reach Earth.
Yutu-2 has driven for years, longer than any earlier lunar rover, and found unusual mantle-like rock.

sites.title: Chang'e 5
left: Lander (the ascender took 1.7 kg of samples home)

facts.text: In December 2020 it returned 1,731 g of the youngest lunar rock yet, from lava about 2 billion years old.
It was the first lunar sample return since Luna 24 in 1976.

sites.title: Chang'e 6
left: Lander (the ascender took 1.9 kg of far-side samples home)

facts.text: In June 2024 it brought back the first samples from the far side of the Moon, from Apollo basin inside the South Pole-Aitken basin.

sites.title: SLIM
left: Two small probes, LEV-1 and LEV-2

facts.text: On 19 January 2024 Japan's lander came down within about 55 m of its target, a pinpoint landing near Shioli crater.
It tipped onto its nose and its solar cells faced the wrong way, yet it worked for days and woke up again after lunar nights.
